sections.title: Mental model — every container is a contract + a memory layout

blocks.md: MAANG probing goes one level under the API: *why* is it that complexity? The answers are always one of three stories: **contiguous memory** (cache-friendly scans), **pointer-chasing nodes** (stable addresses), or **hash buckets** (amortized bets). Map every STL container onto these three and you can derive its table instead of memorizing it.

rows.left: O(1) index · prefetch heaven · binary-searchable · reallocation moves everything

rows.label: Nodes (list/map/set)
rows.left: stable iterators forever · pointer chase = cache misses · no indexing

rows.label: Buckets (unordered_*)
rows.left: avg O(1) probes · worst O(n) chains · rehash storms

blocks.md: **Choose by access pattern, not by habit: index-scan ⇒ vector · ordered queries ⇒ tree · membership storm ⇒ hash (with reserve).**

sections.title: Tree vs hash — the full trade-off script

chain.q: When would you REJECT unordered_map despite average O(1)?
chain.a: Three honest cases: (1) need ORDERED iteration/range queries/lower_bound; (2) worst-case latency contracts — hash's O(n) tail breaks SLAs; (3) adversarial input environments without randomized hashing.

chain.q: What exactly does red-black guarantee vs AVL?
chain.a: RB: height ≤ 2·log(n+1), insert/delete ≤ 3 rotations amortized-cheap — good write-heavy default. AVL: stricter height (≈1.44·log n), faster lookups, costlier rebalances. std::map picked RB for balanced all-round behavior.

chain.q: How do you make hashing robust against hostile inputs?
chain.a: Per-process random seed mixed into std::hash (splitmix64 avalanche): identical inputs collide differently each run → attacker cannot precompute the kill-bucket. Show the struct-hash idiom on demand.
Iteration walks bucket-array THEN chains → Θ(buckets + n). After huge reserve with few elements, iterating is dominated by empty buckets — know this before micro-benchmarks.

blocks.label: splitmix64 custom hash (memorize shape)
blocks.py:
# PYTHON HASH SAFETY: str/bytes hashes are randomized per process
# (PYTHONHASHSEED), so adversarial collision bombs mostly fail already.
# Custom key classes still deserve thought:
class SplitMix:
    def __init__(self): self.seed = id(object())   # per-run variation
    def __call__(self, v):
        x = (v + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        x ^= x >> 30; x = x * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9 & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        x ^= x >> 27; x = x * 0x94d049bb133111eb & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        return x ^ (x >> 31)
# dict with such keys needs explicit wrapper class __hash__/__eq__.

blocks.md: std::priority_queue exposes push/pop/top only. No decrease-key, no arbitrary erase. Every advanced algorithm (Dijkstra, two-heaps median, task schedulers) survives this via **lazy deletion**: obsolete entries stay inside; validity is checked AT POP time.

blocks.label: the canonical guard
blocks.py:
import heapq
pq = []                            # lazy-deletion heap (value, index)
# ... pushes happen freely ...
while pq and stale(pq[0]):
    heapq.heappop(pq)              # discard silently
best = pq[0]

blocks.md: **Cost accounting interviewers love:** lazy deletion may hold O(total pushes) entries, but EVERY entry is pushed once and popped once ⇒ amortized O(log total) per op. State it as amortized analysis, not luck.

Need ONLY the k-th smallest (median, cutoff, percentile)? Full sort pays Θ(n log n) for order you won't read. `nth_element` introselects in **average Θ(n)**: exact element at position n-th, left side all ≤, right side all ≥ — nothing else promised.

items: `reserve()` BEFORE bulk push loops — kills reallocation storms AND keeps pointers valid where you planned capacity
**erase-while-iterating**: use remove-erase (`v.erase(remove_if(...), end())`) or index rewinding — `v.erase(it)` inside range-for is UB territory after invalidation
`emplace_back(args...)` constructs in place — matters for string/struct members
`shrink_to_fit()` is a REQUEST, not a promise — don't build logic on capacity

sections.title: Problem set — L3 hard (idioms under pressure)

items.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
items.statement: Longest run of consecutive integers in O(n) — sorting is the trap answer here.
hints: Insert all into unordered_set.
Only START counting when x−1 absent — sequence heads only.
Each element visited ≤ twice total ⇒ O(n) defended.

solutionCode.label: only start counting from sequence heads

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each element is touched at most twice. Space O(n).

followups.q: Defend the O(n) despite the nested while loop.
followups.a: The inner walk only runs from a sequence head, and it visits each member of that run exactly once. Every value belongs to exactly one run, so across the whole outer loop the inner loop performs at most n steps in total. Each element is touched at most twice — once by the head check, once by a walk — giving O(n), not O(n²).

followups.q: Why is sorting the trap answer?
followups.a: Sorting works and is easy to reach for, but it is O(n log n) and the problem explicitly asks for O(n). Mentioning sorting as the obvious baseline and then rejecting it for the stated constraint is the answer the interviewer wants — silently sorting is what fails.

items.title: Group Anagrams
items.statement: Group words that are anagrams. Then defend your key: sorted-string vs count-vector.
hints: Canonical form = sorted letters OR 26-count tuple.
Key must be EQUALITY-canonical, not human-readable.
Discuss hash-of-custom-struct requirements if avoiding string keys.

solutionCode.label: canonical key: 26-count signature beats sorting

items.complexity: Sorted-string key: O(n · k log k) for n words of length k. Count-vector key: O(n · k).

followups.q: Defend the count key over the sorted-string key.
followups.a: Sorting each word is O(k log k); counting is O(k). For long words the count wins asymptotically. The sorted string is shorter and more readable as a key, and for k ≤ 10 the constants favour it — so state the trade rather than declaring one universally better.

followups.q: Why the `#` separators in the C++ key?
followups.a: Without them, counts 1,11 and 11,1 both concatenate to "111" and two different words collide into one group. A delimiter makes the encoding unambiguous. This is the same reason you cannot naively concatenate fields into a composite key.

items.title: Top K Frequent Elements (O(n) variant)
items.statement: Solve with heap (n log k), then upgrade to frequency buckets for O(n); explain why bucketing is legal here.
hints: freq map → buckets indexed BY frequency (≤ n always).
Walk buckets from high to low collecting k.
Legality: frequencies bounded by n ⇒ linear space.

solutionCode.label: buckets indexed by frequency

items.complexity: Bucketing: O(n) time and space. Heap alternative: O(n log k).

followups.q: Why is bucketing legal here when counting sort usually is not?
followups.a: Counting sort needs a bounded key range. The key here is a frequency, and no frequency can exceed n — the bound is free, given by the input size itself. That is what makes an O(n)-sized bucket array safe, unlike bucketing on the values, which could be any 32-bit integer.

followups.q: When would you still choose the heap?
followups.a: When the data streams and you cannot size an array up front, or when memory matters — the size-k heap is O(k) space against O(n) for buckets. n log k is barely worse than n for small k, so the heap is often the better engineering answer despite the worse asymptotic label.

items.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
items.statement: Count subarrays summing to k in one pass. The hashmap stores PREFIX COUNTS, not positions.
hints: need = prefix − k; add freq[need] before inserting current prefix.
Seed freq[0]=1 for prefixes starting at 0.
Explain why sliding window FAILS with negatives.

solutionCode.label: count prefix sums, not positions
solutionCode.py:
def subarray_sum(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    count = {0: 1}          # the empty prefix, so a whole-array match counts
    prefix = total = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        total += count.get(prefix - k, 0)   # probe BEFORE inserting
        count[prefix] = count.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return total

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one pass, one hash probe each. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why does the map store counts rather than positions?
followups.a: The same prefix sum can occur at many indices, and every one of them starts a valid subarray ending here. You need how many, not where — storing a position would silently keep only the last and undercount. This is the single most common bug on this problem.

followups.q: Why does a sliding window fail with negatives?
followups.a: A window requires the sum to move monotonically as the bounds move. With negatives, extending right can decrease the sum, so "shrink while too big" no longer safely retires the left edge — you can skip valid answers. Prefix sums make no monotonicity assumption.

items.title: K Closest Points to Origin
items.statement: k closest points three ways: full sort, size-k heap, nth_element — compare costs and stability notes.
hints: No sqrt needed — compare squared distances.
nth_element on distance comparator = average O(n).
Follow-up bait: streaming version? (heap wins)

solutionCode.label: nth_element on squared distance — no sqrt, no full sort

items.complexity: nth_element: O(n) average. Size-k heap: O(n log k), O(k) space. Full sort: O(n log n).

followups.a: sqrt is monotonic, so it never changes the ordering — it only costs a floating-point operation per comparison and introduces rounding that can make two genuinely-equal distances compare unequal. Staying in integers keeps the comparison exact.

followups.q: Which of the three would you pick for a stream?
followups.a: The heap. nth_element needs the whole array in memory at once and reorders it destructively; sorting needs it all too. The size-k heap processes one point at a time and holds only k, so it is the only one that survives data you cannot store.

items.title: Design Twitter Timeline Feed
items.statement: Post/follow/unfollow/getNewsFeed(10 latest). Compose user→tweets map + follower sets + k-way merge of recent lists.
hints: Store (time,tweetId) per user, global clock counter.
Feed = merge candidate lists by recency — heap of list-heads.
Unfollow ≠ delete tweets (history persists).

solutionCode.label: global clock + per-user tweet lists + k-way merge of heads

items.complexity: post O(1); follow/unfollow O(1); getNewsFeed O(f log f + 10 log f) for f followees, using a heap over recent-list heads.

followups.q: Why a heap rather than concatenating all followees' tweets and sorting?
followups.a: Concatenating is O(total tweets log total) per feed request. Each per-user list is already sorted by time, so this is a k-way merge of sorted lists — seed the heap with the k heads and pop 10 times. You touch ~k + 10 entries instead of every tweet ever posted.

followups.q: Why must unfollow not delete tweets?
followups.a: The tweets belong to their author, not to the follow relationship. Deleting them would corrupt the feed of every other follower and make re-following lossy. Unfollow removes an edge in the graph; the content store is untouched.

items.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) with DUPLICATES allowed
items.statement: Extend LC380: map value→VECTOR of indices; delete pops an index, swap-to-end patches it.
hints: value→indices vector; lazily skip stale indices on getRandom? No — patch eagerly.
Delete idx: move last element INTO idx, fix its index entry, pop_back.
Edge: deleting the element you just moved — check identity.

solutionCode.label: value -> set of indices; swap-to-end with an identity check
solutionCode.py:
import random


class RandomizedCollection:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vals = []
        self.idx = {}                 # value -> set of positions holding it

    def insert(self, val: int) -> bool:
        is_new = not self.idx.get(val)
        self.idx.setdefault(val, set()).add(len(self.vals))
        self.vals.append(val)
        return is_new

    def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
        positions = self.idx.get(val)
        if not positions:
            return False
        pos = next(iter(positions))
        positions.remove(pos)

        last = len(self.vals) - 1
        if pos != last:               # identity check: skip the self-swap
            moved = self.vals[last]
            self.vals[pos] = moved
            self.idx[moved].discard(last)
            self.idx[moved].add(pos)
        self.vals.pop()
        return True

    def get_random(self) -> int:
        return random.choice(self.vals)

items.complexity: Average O(1) for insert, remove and getRandom. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why is the `pos != last` identity check essential?
followups.a: When you remove the element already at the end, pos == last. Without the guard you would re-insert index `last` into the moved value's index set — but that slot is about to be popped, leaving a dangling index that getRandom can later hit. Deleting the last occurrence of a value is exactly the case that exposes it.

followups.q: Why a set of indices rather than a vector?
followups.a: remove must delete an arbitrary index in O(1), and it must also relocate index `last` to `pos` for the moved value. A vector makes "erase this specific index" O(size of the list); a hash set makes both operations O(1) average. Order among the indices is irrelevant.

revisionCard: Three layout stories: contiguous / node-chase / hash-buckets — derive costs from them
Reject hash when order needed, latency tails matter, or adversaries lack a randomized hash
Lazy deletion: push freely, validate at pop — amortized cost argument required
nth_element: exact k-th + partitioned sides at avg Θ(n) — selection ≠ sorting
reserve() before storms · remove-erase idiom · emplace_back for heavy members
Sequence-start detection trick makes LC128 linear — visit-count defense
Prefix-COUNT maps (freq[0]=1 seed) solve subarray-sum-k where windows fail (negatives)

glossary.def: Relaxed-height BST backing map/set; rotation-cheap writes.
Bit-mixing (splitmix64) making outputs decorrelate from input patterns.
Leaving invalidated heap entries, filtering them during pops; validity checked lazily.
Quickselect + fallback strategy behind nth_element; average-linear selection.
remove_if compacts survivors; erase commits truncation — the safe filter pattern.
Normalized representation (sorted chars, count-tuple) making equivalence classes collide.
When a value is provably ≤ n, index buckets by it for linear grouping.
